1 2 3 Longitudinal motor-imagery EEG decoding: Frozen baselines, supervised recalibration, and task-measurement reliability 4 5 Short title: Longitudinal EEG decoding with limited recalibration labels 6 Ziyuan Zhu 7 College of Artificial Intelligence Medicine, Chongqing Medical University, Chongqing, China 8 Corresponding author: Ziyuan Zhu; zzy2630816871@gmail.com 9 ORCID: https://orcid.org/0009-0005-1153-4926 1 10 Abstract 11 Supervised recalibration can update a brain–computer interface classifier, its spatial filters, or both. 12 We compared these choices in 18 participant records across six sessions of Kumar2024 (NEMAR 13 nm000177/v1.0.5). A frozen protocol separated six development participants from a predefined 12- 14 participant primary cohort. Source-only CSP/LDA was compared with classifier-only recalibration 15 and full CSP/LDA refitting; the two update methods used the same 19 or 20 current-session support 16 labels. Always-frozen EEGNet retained three fixed seeds. The primary full-refit-minus-frozen con- 17 trast was 7.42 percentage points (95% participant-bootstrap interval 2.49–12.48). The secondary 18 same-label-budget full-refit-minus-LDA-only contrast was 5.47 points (2.17–8.91), whereas LDA- 19 only recalibration versus frozen decoding remained uncertain. Three of the 12 participants had de- 20 creases of 0.20–5.82 points. An exploratory amplitude-QC analysis retained complete five-session 21 endpoints for ten participants, with a full-minus-frozen contrast of 5.96 points (0.99–11.24); missing 22 classes and conditional selection limit this comparison. In the primary cohort, EEGNet source-query 23 balanced accuracy was 52.92% and target BA 51.58%. Weak discrimination was therefore already 24 present within the source session; the target score alone does not identify the contribution of cross- 25 session drift. Reliability probes did not establish a useful adaptation gate. The documented export 26 convention anchors five-second windows at the visual cue, but their trial-level phase composition 27 was not reconstructed. Full refitting improved the cohort average under the specified support-label 28 budget, with substantial individual variation. Prior test exposure makes the follow-up analyses ex- 29 ploratory. The findings concern released task-label windows, rather than isolated sustained imagery, 30 human skill retention or clinical efficacy. 2 31 Introduction 32 Longitudinal motor-imagery brain–computer interface (BCI) decoding must account for changes in 33 recording distributions and in the relation between signals and task labels. Nonstationarity, limited 34 calibration data and evaluation design remain recurring challenges [1]. Common spatial patterns 35 (CSP) and linear discriminant analysis (LDA) offer a conventional setting in which spatial repre- 36 sentation and classification can be updated separately [2,3]. A current-session label budget may 37 improve decoding, but it does not establish that every participant or session benefits from updating. 38 The acquisition study used incremental covariance recentering with a Riemannian minimum- 39 distance-to-mean classifier. 40 class-prototype updates during the first run of each session; a separate pseudo-online analysis 41 extended recentering to CSP and a linear discriminant classifier [4,5]. These procedures establish 42 important precedents for adaptation and session-start calibration, but differ from refitting CSP and 43 LDA on the same small labeled support set. 44 Our primary comparison asks how much full refitting improves decoding over a completely frozen 45 CSP/LDA pipeline when approximately 20 current-session labels are available. This total contrast 46 combines access to support labels with updates to both stages. The secondary comparison, full refit- 47 ting versus LDA-only recalibration, more directly addresses the additional contribution of updating 48 spatial filters because the two methods use identical labels. We retain this predefined hierarchy 49 rather than promote the secondary comparison after seeing its result. A further question is whether 50 the available task measurements can support reliable decisions about when to update. 51 Distribution alignment is a related but different strategy. Euclidean alignment and Riemannian 52 transfer frameworks reduce between-domain mismatch before or within decoding [6,7]. Such ap- 53 proaches are relevant alternatives, not baselines that were implemented here. A covariance distance 54 or task-score measurement alone neither reproduces those methods nor establishes that a policy Its personally adjusted recentering framework added supervised 3 55 based on it improves decoding. Likewise, decoder accuracy is not interchangeable with a user’s 56 mental-imagery skill [8]. This secondary analysis evaluates stored task labels rather than the origi- 57 nal study’s online interventions or acquired skills. 58 Earlier work examined unsupervised adaptation of LDA in motor-imagery BCIs [9]. EEG data- 59 space adaptation instead estimated supervised or unsupervised channel-space transformations be- 60 fore applying an existing CSP/LDA decoder; one evaluated setting used the first 20 target trials for 61 adaptation [10]. These methods update different components and were not implemented as com- 62 parators here. 63 EEGNet supplies a compact neural reference [11], but identical query trials do not equalize source- 64 validation labels, target support or optimization. We retain every fixed seed and class-collapsed 65 outcome and examine saved learning histories to interpret this small-source setting. We also trace 66 the exported events to their task semantics: a complete data window is not automatically a complete 67 imagery phase. The study contributes a component-level baseline comparison and an assessment of 68 whether task measurements are adequate for individual update decisions. The reliability evidence 69 was insufficient to validate such a decision rule. 70 Materials and methods 71 Data source, original study and ethical status 72 This study used the publicly available Kumar2024 derivative, NEMAR nm000177/v1.0.5 [12], as- 73 sociated with the original study and its correction [4,5]. Invalid age placeholders and unresolved original training- protocol 92 membership preclude demographic or intervention-subgroup claims. 93 Exported windows, task-phase meaning and chronological partition 94 The frozen analysis identified 7,200 exported left/right event identities and used five-second inter- 95 vals beginning at their annotated onset. Forty-four intervals ended at the recording boundary before 96 five seconds; they were preserved and excluded without padding or replacement, leaving 7,156 97 complete windows. Completeness here refers to available recorded samples, not to five seconds of 98 continuous motor imagery. 99 The original author-supplied codebook defines 769/770 as left/right cue markers and distinct 5 100 7691/7701 markers as task-period starts [14]. The MOABB Kumar adapter [15] maps 769/770 to 101 left/right and declares [0,5] seconds; the derivative’s class annotations and fixed/clipped durations 102 agree with this documented export convention. The precise historical converter commit and 103 the original trial-level marker arrays were not independently replayed. The original Methods 104 describe a 1.5-second cue preceding feedback, with an offline task duration of five seconds and 105 online feedback lasting at most seven seconds, followed by result and rest. These sources support 106 a cue-anchored task-label export convention; they do not independently certify the phase 107 alignment of every analyzed trial. A nominal cue-anchored window includes the cue interval and 108 at most the subsequent 3.5 seconds; early online termination could introduce later phases. Their 109 trial-level proportions cannot be measured without the original marker sequence and a verified 110 clock mapping. We did not reconstruct these phases from labels or alter any window. 111 All 44 short intervals occur on the last event of an online recording and stop at the audited EDF end. 112 This is a recording-boundary relationship, not evidence that exactly 44 tasks ended early. Neither 113 variable task duration by itself nor this boundary check establishes a sample-indexing error. The 114 original results are retained as decoding of the released task-label windows. Derivative 129 timestamp order was checked; absolute calendar accuracy was not independently established. 130 Preprocessing and fixed amplitude-QC flag 131 Each event independently underwent common-average referencing across 22 channels, fourth-order 132 8–30 Hz Butterworth zero-phase filtering and polyphase resampling from 512 to 128 Hz, yielding 133 22 × 640 float32 values in volts. These epoch-local operations learned no held-out statistics. Zero- 134 phase filtering defines an offline analysis; it neither proves real-time operation nor removes a cue 135 or feedback contribution. No threshold or preprocessing parameter was selected from the new sensitivity results. 140 Decoders and information budgets 141 The CPU pipeline used four-component CSP with Ledoit–Wolf regularization, log mean-square fea- 142 tures and norm_trace=False , followed by shrinkage LDA ( solver=lsqr , automatic shrinkage). 143 One prespecified configuration was used. Source-only CSP and LDA stayed fixed. Recalibration 144 retained source CSP and refitted LDA with source training plus current support; full refitting up- 145 dated both stages using that same union. Validation and query identities were excluded from all 7 146 CPU fitting and parameter selection. 147 EEGNet used the frozen Braindecode architecture (F1=4, D=2, F2=8, dropout 0.5), Adam at learn- 148 ing rate 0.001, batch size 16 and a maximum of 100 epochs. Channel means and scales were fitted to 149 source training only. Source-validation cross entropy selected the earliest best epoch with patience 150 15; the complete selected state was restored. All three seeds (20261012, 20261013 and 20261014) 151 were retained for each participant. The 54 completed source fits used 2,871 epochs and 8,613 opti- 152 mizer steps. No source fit was repeated for query evaluation. The original 10 198 source/support/validation data and fitted models were not cleaned or retrained by this procedure. 199 Post-review paired statistical checks 200 In response to review, we added an exploratory check of four contrasts using the saved participant 201 endpoints: full refit minus frozen, full refit minus LDA-only and LDA-only minus frozen in the pre- 202 defined 12 participants, and full refit minus frozen in the ten participants eligible for the unflagged 203 sensitivity. We enumerated all 2 𝑛 sign assignments and used the absolute mean paired difference 204 as the two-sided statistic. Differences were expressed in BA units; values within 10 −12 of the ob- 205 served tail boundary were included. This reference distribution assumes independent participant 206 differences with sign symmetry about zero. It is not a test based on randomized assignment and is 207 not assumption-free population inference. 208 We report unadjusted values and Holm adjustment across these four checks. S1 212 Text, S11 documents enumeration, rounding diagnostics and the distinction between this test and 213 the original percentile intervals. 214 Task measurements and development-only reliability 215 The descriptive drift analysis compared each target session with the independent source query. 216 A source-trained task axis was the normalized difference between class means in standardized 217 44-dimensional mu/beta log-power coordinates; one-dimensional Wasserstein distance measured 218 change along that fixed axis. Covariance-shape change was measured relative to a source-training 219 Riemannian reference in a fixed 21-dimensional common-average-reference basis, after trace nor- 11 220 malization and fixed shrinkage. This shape proxy does not measure all distributional changes or 221 absolute amplitude. Target labels did not define either drift predictor. The outcome was target- 222 minus-source frozen-decoder BA; target-labeled class summaries were retrospective descriptions. 223 These pooled associations combine within- and between-participant variation; all five changes for 224 a participant also share the same small source-query baseline. Participant- block resampling pre- 225 serves this clustering but does not separate those sources of variation or remove error in the shared 226 baseline. 227 The task-measurement reliability probes used only development source training and predeclared sup- 228 port. Fixed power, PCA and supervised CSP-score measurements were evaluated with source-run 229 grouping, support split halves and cyclic-label controls. The controls are phase-alignment sensi- 230 tivities, not formal permutation p values. Separately, the remaining-cohort drift associations were 231 pre-frozen descriptive analyses, not policy selection. No diagnostic selected an adaptation threshold 232 or used query outcomes to choose a policy. 233 Source-run probes trained on one 20-event source run and evaluated the other, then reversed the 234 roles. Learned transformations were fitted within each source training fold; a transform fitted on 235 all 40 events was not reused to score a held-out source run. The supervised diagnostic refitted both 236 CSP and LDA within each fold. For support descriptions, the existing 40-event source models and 237 source-fitted coordinate scales were held fixed. Each class was split into chronological halves within 238 the current support run, without query access. Vector cosines and signed source-score contrasts 239 summarized agreement between the halves; agreement did not itself establish a useful adaptation 240 decision. 241 Cyclic label controls retained the prescribed run grouping and enumerated label phases. They were 242 not random-label exchangeability tests. All 240 supervised CSP/LDA fold/rotation pipelines and 243 all associated controls were retained. Supplementary Methods S4–S6 define the coordinate scales, 12 244 half sizes, score orientation, control enumeration and handling of degenerate cases. 245 Saved training review and AI-assisted preparation 246 We examined all saved epoch-level training/validation histories, selected epochs, fixed seeds and 247 existing source/target query metrics without loading checkpoints or repeating inference. Training 248 losses were accumulated in training mode while parameters changed; validation losses were com- 249 puted after the epoch in evaluation mode. Unflagged windows remain 387 unreviewed for other artifacts. 388 Exploratory post-review paired tests 389 The exhaustive sign-flip results are shown in Table 5. For the primary contrast, 80 of 4,096 as- 390 signments were at least as extreme as observed, giving an unadjusted p value of 0.01953 and a 391 four-comparison Holm value of 0.05859. The unflagged ten-participant contrast gave 78/1,024, or 392 0.07617, despite its positive percentile-bootstrap interval. The two procedures use different refer- 393 ence constructions; excluding zero from this percentile interval is not equivalent to a p value below 394 0.05 in this sign-flip test. These post-review checks supplement the estimates without changing 395 their predefined hierarchy. 396 Table 5. Post-review exploratory participant-level sign-flip checks. 20 Paired contrast and subset Full refit − frozen, Participants Unadjusted two-sided p Holm p, four checks 12 0.01953 0.05859 12 0.01025 0.04102 12 0.26123 0.26123 10 0.07617 0.15234 original primary cohort Full refit − LDA-only, same primary cohort LDA-only − frozen, same primary cohort Full refit − frozen, unflagged eligible subset 397 All assignments were enumerated with the same prespecified numerical tolerance for this post- 398 review computation. Holm adjustment concerns only these four checks; it does not remedy their 399 outcome-informed introduction or validate a new adaptation rule. Original effect sizes and intervals 400 remain unchanged. 401 Discussion 402 Increment beyond established supervised recalibration 403 The component comparison is the main addition to this longitudinal resource. Under the same 19/20- 404 label support budget, full refitting exceeded LDA-only recalibration by a secondary mean of 5.47 21 405 points. This suggests that updating CSP can add value in this particular pipeline; the primary 7.42- 406 point contrast instead measures the total change from a frozen pipeline to full supervised refitting. 407 Neither identifies a physiological mechanism or establishes a universal recommendation to update. 408 The distinction from the acquisition study matters. Its GR and PAR frameworks both adapted co- 409 variance recentering online; PAR additionally updated Riemannian class prototypes using first-run 410 labels. Their group comparison does not estimate LDA-only updating versus a fully frozen decoder, 411 and a nonsignificant group difference is not evidence of equivalence. Its separate GR-CSP extension 412 also differs from our supervised component-refitting comparison [4,5]. Similarly, LDA adaptation 413 and EEG data-space adaptation update different parts of the decoding process [9,10]. Their results 414 are relevant background, not additional experiments or independent confirmation of our contrast. 415 Useful adaptation requires more than a cohort-average improvement. The observed task-score ori- 416 entation was inconsistent within some support runs, and the prespecified drift proxies had wide 417 associations with performance. No threshold, gate or new strategy was chosen from these data. 418 Alignment methods remain important comparators for a separately reviewed study [6,7]; they can- 419 not be retrospectively credited to this benchmark. Reliable individual update decisions would re- 420 quire a separately frozen, group-aware nested development evaluation against equal-label-budget 421 controls. 422 Window semantics and signal quality limit interpretation 423 The strongest qualification is that the recorded endpoint labels classify cue-anchored windows 424 in a motor-imagery experiment, not a verified sustained imagery segment. Cue perception, feed- 425 back, ocular/muscle activity and online termination-related phases could contribute. The recording- 426 boundary exclusion of 44 short events neither repairs nor estimates those contributions. A fu- 427 ture phase-specific analysis would first require matched original task-start/end markers and sam- 22 428 ple clocks, a preserved new eligibility ledger and a separately reviewed fixed window. It must not 429 search window positions for better scores or overwrite the present benchmark. 430 The amplitude sensitivity directly addresses saved decoding outcomes, unlike a power-only QC 431 description. Its positive complete-case contrasts and lack of a single-participant sign reversal narrow 432 some simple influence explanations. However, two of twelve primary participants lose a valid five- 433 session endpoint, conditioning on amplitude changes the sample and small class counts remain. 434 Flagged fit and validation examples still influence the stored models. These limitations preclude 435 labeling the results artifact-free or robust to all signal-quality problems. The substantially different 436 cue/task meanings also cannot be resolved by an amplitude threshold. 437 Neural baseline and statistical scope 438 EEGNet’s weak held-out source-session score is the first interpretive constraint. Its target score does 439 not by itself identify the effect of cross-session drift. Saved histories show training loss reduction 440 without consistent validation benefit, heterogeneous stopping and seed variation. These support a 441 limited small-source benchmark, without proving a unique cause or that deep learning is unsuitable 442 for this task. Parameter choice, additional source labels or alignment would be new experiments, 443 not permissible post-query fixes. 444 There are 18 published participant identities, 12 in the primary comparison and six in reliability 445 probes, not 54 independent participants. The development allocation preceded these results and 446 was retained even though it did not validate an update gate; its +3.25-point contrast was reported 447 separately, without pooling it into the primary analysis. The primary interval spans approximately 448 2.5 to 12.5 points and three participants had decreases. These data describe a cohort average but 449 provide little precision for deciding who should receive an update. Bootstrap intervals condition 450 on these participants, fixed windows and fitted models. Earlier test exposure makes follow-up 23 451 QC, neural comparisons and manuscript-driven summaries exploratory. Source metadata, protocol 452 membership and biological independence also have unresolved qualifications. Offline task-label 453 accuracy does not measure acquired BCI skill, human learning or clinical benefit [8]. 454 Conclusions 455 Full CSP/LDA refitting improved the cohort-average endpoint under the specified support-label 456 budget, whereas LDA-only recalibration versus frozen decoding remained uncertain. The secondary 457 same-label-budget advantage over LDA-only updating and retained individual/session variation mo- 458 tivate measuring when adaptation is useful, but no reliable task-aware gate was validated. Weak in- 459 dependent source-query EEGNet performance precedes its weak target result. New QC sensitivity 460 is qualified by incomplete class coverage and the continued influence of flagged fitting data. The 461 present evidence supports transparent interpretation of released cue-anchored task-label windows, 462 not isolated sustained imagery, skill retention or clinical validity. 463 Data and code availability 464 The source EEG is publicly available as NEMAR nm000177/v1.0.5, DOI 10.82901/ne- 465 mar.nm000177.v1.0.5, under its stated CC BY 4.0 terms [12].
